text.en: On a sunny day your shadow follows you. In the evening it grows long. Light and shadows are linked, and mirrors can send light back.

Luminous objects make their own light, such as the Sun, a torch and a candle. Non-luminous objects like the Moon only reflect light.
Transparent materials let light through clearly. Translucent materials transmit and scatter some light. Opaque materials block light from passing through. Light travels in straight lines.
A shadow forms where an object blocks light. Its outline depends on the object, light and screen. With the light source and screen fixed, moving the object towards the source usually makes its shadow bigger. A pinhole camera uses a tiny hole to make an upside-down image on a screen because light moves in straight lines.
Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A plane mirror forms an image of the same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and it shows mirror reversal: your raised right hand looks like the image’s raised left hand.
Luminous objects make their own light, such as the Sun, a torch and a candle. Non-luminous objects like the Moon only reflect light.

board.text: Sources of light

text.en: Transparent materials let light through clearly. Translucent materials let some light through but scatter it. Opaque materials block light from passing through.

board.text: Light and materials

text.en: Light travels in straight lines.
A shadow forms where an object blocks light. Its outline depends on the shape and position of the object, the light and the screen.

board.text: Shadows

text.en: With the lamp and screen fixed, a shadow usually grows when the object moves closer to the lamp and shrinks when it moves closer to the screen.
A pinhole camera uses a tiny hole to make an upside-down image on a screen because light moves in straight lines.
Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

board.text: Reflection

text.en: A plane mirror gives an upright, same-size image. It appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. A raised hand seems to belong to the image’s opposite hand.
A glowing bulb gives off light. A book under the bulb becomes visible because light from the bulb reflects from the book into your eyes.

board.text: Source makes light; reflector returns it

text.en: The Moon looks bright in the sky because sunlight reflects from its surface. It is visible without being a source of its own visible light.

board.text: The Moon reflects sunlight

text.en: The Sun and some fireflies make their own light. A switched-on torch uses electricity to produce light.

board.text: A source can be natural or artificial

text.en: Line up holes in three cards. A torch behind the first card can be seen through the last card when all the holes are aligned.

board.text: Three card holes in one line

text.en: When a hole is moved sideways, the straight path is blocked. The beam does not turn to find the new opening.

board.text: Shift one hole sideways

text.en: Put a clean clear cover over a printed word. If the outlines are still easy to see, the cover lets light through clearly.

board.text: Clear sheet: fine detail is visible

text.en: Tracing paper scatters the light that passes through it. You see a brightness but lose fine details.

board.text: Tracing paper: light without clear details

text.en: Thick cardboard is opaque. Light can reflect from its front, but does not pass through to the other side.

board.text: Cardboard: blocks light through it

text.en: Place a card between a torch and a screen. Rays stopped by the card leave a darker region on the screen.

board.text: A shadow needs a source and blocker

text.en: A flat round disc gives a broad round shadow when it faces the light. Turn it edge-on and the shadow becomes thin.

board.text: Rotate the object to change its outline

text.en: Print on a card may be visible when you look at the card. The shadow instead shows where the card stopped the light.

board.text: A shadow cannot show a printed pattern

text.en: Compare the shadow with the card near the lamp and then near the screen. Keep the other distances fixed to isolate the effect.

board.text: Fixed lamp and screen: move only the card

text.en: One object can block rays from two sources at different positions. That can make two different dark regions on the screen.

board.text: Two lamps can form two shadows

text.en: A mirror reflects rays in a regular way. A rough wall reflects rays in many directions, so it usually does not show a clear image.

board.text: Smooth surfaces give clear reflections

text.en: At the point where a ray hits the mirror, draw a line at right angles to the surface. That line is called the normal.

board.text: Draw the normal at 90 degrees

text.en: If a ray arrives at thirty degrees to the normal, it leaves at thirty degrees from the normal on the other side.

board.text: Measure both angles from the normal

text.en: An object twenty centimetres in front of the mirror has an image that appears twenty centimetres behind it. The object and image are forty centimetres apart.

board.text: Mirror: equal distances on either side

text.en: Reflected rays reach your eyes as if they came from behind the mirror. You cannot catch the apparent image on a screen placed there.

board.text: A virtual mirror image

text.en: Trace a ray from the top of an object through the pinhole to the lower screen. A ray from the bottom reaches the upper screen.

board.text: Pinhole: rays cross

text.en: The rays reach the screen itself, making a real, inverted image. A bright object in a safe indoor setup makes it easier to see.

board.text: A screen catches the pinhole image

text.en: One mirror sends light down the tube. The other sends it towards your eye, letting you see above an obstacle.

board.text: A periscope uses two reflections

text.en: Facing mirrors can reflect the same coloured pieces more than once. As the pieces move, the repeated pattern changes.

board.text: A kaleidoscope repeats reflections

problem.en: A girl stands 1 m in front of a mirror. How far is her image from her?

text.en: The image is as far behind the mirror.
1 m behind the mirror, so 2 m from her.

problem.en: A torch and screen stay fixed. Which move usually enlarges a card’s shadow?

text.en: Move the card closer to the torch.

why.en: It intercepts rays that would spread over a larger part of the screen.

text.en: Keep the light and screen where they were.

why.en: The card’s position is the only change being tested.

problem.en: Where does light from the top of a toy land in a pinhole camera?

text.en: Draw a straight ray from the toy’s top through the tiny hole.

why.en: The ray continues in a straight line past the hole.

text.en: It reaches the lower part of the screen.

why.en: The paths cross at the hole, so the image is upside down.

requiredIdeas.en: An opaque object blocks the straight path of light.

points.en: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
Plane mirror image is same size and laterally inverted.
